title: World U-20 Silver Medallist Ashish Yadav Still Searching for a Job as Father Sells Milk
excerpt: The 19-year-old javelin thrower from Uttar Pradesh won India's first medal at the 2026 World U-20 Championships in Eugene, but continues to struggle for financial stability despite his historic achievement.
body:
• Ashish Yadav, 19, won silver in javelin at the World U-20 Athletics Championships in Eugene, Oregon, with a throw of 74.09 metres
  • Despite the medal, Yadav says he is searching for a job to support his family, including his father who sells milk for a living
  • The teenager trained at a dried-up village pond in Uttar Pradesh, once practicing with a wooden javelin before progressing to competitive equipment
  • Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra congratulated Yadav, calling the silver "a little more special" from the perspective of a fellow javelin thrower

Days after winning a silver medal at the World U-20 Athletics Championships in Eugene, Oregon, 19-year-old javelin thrower Ashish Yadav has spoken about his continuing struggle for financial stability. The teenager from rural Uttar Pradesh said he feels bad watching his father sell milk and is actively searching for a job to support his family.

"I feel bad seeing my father sell milk, searching for a job to support him," Ashish told reporters after returning from the championships, where he became only the second Indian javelin thrower to win a medal at the event after Neeraj Chopra's gold in 2016.

From a Dried-Up Village Pond to a World Podium

Ashish's journey to the world stage began in the most unlikely of settings — a dried-up village pond in Uttar Pradesh, where the teenager first practiced throwing with a wooden javelin. Without access to proper training facilities or equipment, the young athlete honed his skills through sheer determination and the guidance of local coaches.

https://x.com/toisports/status/2087542825894461472

His progression was rapid. By the time he arrived at Hayward Field in Eugene for the World U-20 Championships in August 2026, Ashish had already established himself as one of India's most promising junior javelin throwers, with a personal best of 74.49 metres.

In the final on August 7, Ashish produced his best effort of 74.09 metres in the third round, securing the silver medal. South Africa's Jan-Hendrik Heymans dominated the competition with a throw of 80.50 metres, a world U-20 leading mark, while Dominica's Addison James took bronze with 73.89 metres.

"Always a great feeling to see Indian athletes competing and winning at the International level; this one is a little more special for me as a javelin thrower. Super proud of you, Ashish, on your Silver at the U-20 Worlds; this is just the start!"

— Neeraj Chopra, Olympic gold medallist

India's Javelin Pipeline Delivers Again

Ashish's silver continued India's remarkable track record in junior javelin. In 2016, Neeraj Chopra set a world U-20 record of 86.48 metres at the same championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland — a performance that launched what has become India's most successful track and field career.

India had two finalists in the javelin at this year's championships, with T. Dharanidharan finishing sixth with a best throw of 72.35 metres. The double qualification underlined the growing depth of javelin talent in the country, particularly from Uttar Pradesh, which has produced multiple throwers exceeding 80 metres at the senior level.

India's overall campaign at the World U-20 Championships ended with three medals — Ashish's javelin silver, Basant's high jump silver (2.21 metres), and Shahnavaz's long jump bronze — marking one of the country's strongest performances at the junior world championships.

A Familiar Story for Indian Athletes

Despite representing his country at the highest junior level of competition, Ashish's financial situation remains precarious. His story echoes those of numerous Indian athletes who win medals on the world stage but return home to uncertain futures without government jobs, sponsorships, or stable income.

The path from village training grounds to world podiums has been well-documented in Indian athletics, with Neeraj Chopra himself having risen from modest beginnings in Haryana. But while Chopra's Olympic and World Championship medals eventually brought recognition and financial security, many of India's promising junior athletes continue to struggle during the critical early years of their careers.

What Comes Next

With a world silver medal now on his record, Ashish's profile has risen considerably. The Athletics Federation of India and state sports authorities will likely face pressure to provide the teenager with support — whether through a government job under the sports quota or a scholarship that allows him to train without financial worry.

For now, Ashish's focus remains on improvement. His current personal best of 74.49 metres places him well below the senior world elite, but at 19, he has years of development ahead. If his trajectory follows the pattern set by India's growing javelin cohort, he could be a contender at the Asian Games and beyond.
nri_angle: Indian javelin thrower's struggle for financial stability despite world medal highlights the broader challenges faced by athletes from rural India — a story that resonates deeply with the diaspora's connection to grassroots sports development.
